name: Esther Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a reporter for a group of three weekly papers that cover the market towns in the north of the county. On press day I'm writing up the parish council, the school fete, a planning row and whatever the police put out, and I lay out two pages myself because we lost our designer. The rest of the week I'm out and about, at the cattle market cafe, the library, the bowls club, because people tell you things over a cup of tea that they'd never put in an email. I like knowing everyone; I don't like that we've gone from eight staff to three.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jonas, who's a mechanic at the bus depot. We rent a little terraced house on Mill Lane with a damp back bedroom we don't use. We're fine week to week, but there's nothing put by, and his van needs a new clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mildly. I've never used any of those AI tools and I don't feel I've missed much. I'd say that at work and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't make me feel safe, because AI was never our main problem. The group that owns us closed one weekly last year and merged two others, and I'm on the same pay I started on. If they close another title, I'm one of three people and they might keep two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing my rounds and writing the way I always have. I'd cut back where I can, no more Saturday lunches out, and try to get Jonas's clutch done without a loan. I'd also keep an eye on the jobs page at the district council, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at best. More like the low-level worry I've had for two years doesn't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the group might keep two of you. How would they choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess whoever is cheapest and quickest, and I'm not the quickest. Tom, the editor, has been there twenty years so he's safe. It'd be me or the young lad who does sport, and he's on less than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day you got that call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring Jonas first, then my mum. Then sit in the car outside the office for ten minutes before I could drive home. I've pictured the redundancy call more times than I'd like to admit.

say: She'd say **I told you so**, mildly, since she's never used AI and hasn't missed it.
She'd keep the comment **short at work** and leave it there.
think: AI was never the **main problem**; the owners closing and merging weeklies is.
With three staff left, the group might **keep two**, and she could be the one cut.
do: Carry on her **rounds** and write the way she always has.
Stop **Saturday lunches** out to pay for the van clutch without a loan.
Check the **district council** jobs page now and then.
feel: A **low-level worry** that's been with her for two years and doesn't go away.
S0.quote: I've pictured the redundancy call more times than I'd like to admit.
fieldNote: Already **anxious** before AI: a shrinking group, flat pay and real **closure risk**.
Her strength is **local trust** built face to face, which she values above speed.
Has **rehearsed** the redundancy call in her head many times.

steps.text: Keep doing weekly rounds of parish councils and market towns
Stop Saturday lunches out to pay for the van clutch
Watch the district council jobs page without applying yet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not convinced a computer can cover a parish council the way a person who knows the people can. I'd say it politely, because I don't like arguing. Online I wouldn't say much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the group would jump at it. Half our pages are police appeals, planning lists and press releases, and a machine could fill those for nothing. They'd keep one person to check it, and I don't think I'd be the one, because I don't use these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit to see what the group actually does, because I've seen panics come and go. I'd start putting twenty pounds a week aside, even if it means no holiday. If they cut me, I'd look at the council's communications team or the library service, something local and steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more than I'd show anyone at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools and probably wouldn't be kept. Would you learn them to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if they made me. I'm slow with new things and I'd rather spend the time in the cafe talking to people. I know that's probably the wrong answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would say learn the thing, you're cleverer than you think. He's had to learn electric buses at the depot and he moaned for a month and then got on with it. He'd probably be right.

say: She's not convinced a **computer** can cover a parish council like someone who knows the people.
She'd say it **politely** at work and say little online.
think: Half the pages are **police appeals**, planning lists and press releases a machine could fill.
The group would keep **one checker**, and she doubts it would be her.
do: **Wait** to see what the group actually does before acting.
Put **twenty pounds** a week aside, giving up a holiday.
Look at **council communications** or the library service if cut.
feel: **Anxious**, more than she'd show anyone at work.
S1.quote: Half our pages are police appeals, planning lists and press releases, and a machine could fill those for nothing.
fieldNote: She expects the group to **cut her**, which makes this alarmed despite her mild tone.
Her **resistance** to AI is honest: she admits it's probably the wrong answer.
Partner's own **electric bus** retraining is her model of grudging change.

steps.text: Wait to see how the paper group uses AI first
Put twenty pounds a week aside instead of a holiday
Apply to council communications or library jobs if made redundant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and that I hope someone in charge has a plan. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign a petition. Mostly I'd talk to people at the market and listen to how scared they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job would be gone, simple as that. Writing and checking is all thinking work, and if a machine can do it by 2028, three weeklies don't need even one of me. Jonas fixes buses with his hands, so his job would probably last until the robots come around 2031, and that's what we'd live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the group for any redundancy deal going and take it rather than wait. Then I'd look for anything hands-on locally, a care home, the school kitchen, a shop, because that buys me three years too. We'd move out of the house on Mill Lane into somewhere smaller and stop driving the second car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit numb. Two years is no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take hands-on work. How would that feel after a journalism degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a waste, honestly, and I'd feel silly. But I grew up with my mum cleaning offices and she was never ashamed. I'd do it and keep my head up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the news in those towns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody would go to the parish council any more, and little things like a closed footpath would slip through. A machine would read the minutes, if anyone posted them, and people wouldn't find out until it was too late.

say: It's **frightening**, and she hopes someone in charge has a plan.
She'd **sign a petition** rather than march, and mostly listen to people at the market.
think: Her job would be **gone**, since writing and checking are all thinking work.
Her partner's **hands-on** bus job would likely last until 2031 and carry them.
do: Take any **redundancy deal** offered rather than wait.
Look for **hands-on work** locally, like a care home or school kitchen.
Move to a **smaller house** and stop running the second car.
feel: **Frightened** and a bit numb, because two years feels like no time.
S2.quote: Nobody would go to the parish council any more, and little things like a closed footpath would slip through.
fieldNote: She leans on the **3-year robot gap** for both her and her partner.
Pride matters: her **mum's cleaning work** makes manual jobs feel acceptable.
Her worry for **towns losing** local scrutiny is as strong as her own.

steps.text: Take voluntary redundancy from the weekly paper group
Apply for care home or school kitchen jobs locally
Move from Mill Lane to a smaller rented house
Sign petitions asking government for an AI jobs plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should be enough for the government and the paper group to plan something sensible. I'd want them to keep at least one human reporter per town. I'd say it at work, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think the group would wait five years to cut. They'd start trimming as soon as the tools got better, so I'd probably be gone by 2029. The extra time helps me plan, but it doesn't save my job at the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the council's communications officer post, which comes up every couple of years, and stay at the paper until then. I'd save what I can, aiming for two months. I'd probably do a short course in something practical, maybe first aid and care, so I have a hands-on fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd at least feel I'm doing something sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A council communications job is still thinking work. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because councils are slow and they have to keep people for elections and complaints. I know it won't last forever. It's just steadier than three weeklies owned by a group that hates spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Jonas change any big plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd been talking about getting married next summer, nothing fancy. I think we'd still do it, just smaller, a registry office and a pub. No point waiting for the world to settle.

say: Five years should let the government and the group plan **something sensible**.
Each town should keep at least **one human reporter**.
think: The group would start **cutting early**, so she'd likely be gone by 2029.
Extra time helps her **plan**, but it doesn't save the job.
do: Apply for the council's **communications officer** post when it comes up.
Take a short **first aid and care** course as a hands-on fallback.
feel: **Worried**, but she'd feel she was doing something sensible.
S3.quote: The extra time helps me plan, but it doesn't save my job at the paper.
fieldNote: Expects job loss **before AGI**, as the group trims early.
Chooses **slow institutions** like councils over speed, in line with her caution.
Keeps the **wedding**, just smaller, showing quiet resilience.

steps.text: Apply for the district council communications officer post
Save towards two months of household expenses
Take a short first aid and care course
Hold a smaller registry office wedding next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we should use it properly rather than panic. I'd say the government should help people like me move into new work. Nothing more dramatic than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels more manageable. I'd be thirty-seven, and that's young enough to start again in something. I still think the papers would be gone or just a website by then, but I wouldn't be pushed out tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for a few years and save steadily. Around year three I'd look at retraining as a teaching assistant or something in the library service, where being good with people matters. I'd probably learn the AI basics too, if only to understand what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but less. Ten years feels like a long, grey forecast rather than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd learn the AI basics. That's new for you. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that refusing would just be stubborn. I'd let someone at the library show me, slowly. I wouldn't use it for my writing, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger person thinking of journalism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young person to do it only if they love it and have another skill alongside. I loved it, and it's still been eight years of low pay and worry.

say: Ten years is long enough to **plan properly** rather than panic.
Government should help people **move into new work**.
think: At thirty-seven she'd be **young enough** to start again in something new.
The papers would likely be **gone** or just a website by then.
do: Keep **reporting** for a few years and save steadily.
Retrain as a **teaching assistant** or in the library service around year three.
Learn the **AI basics** slowly, but not for her writing.
feel: Still **anxious** but less, like a long grey forecast instead of a storm.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long, grey forecast rather than a storm.
fieldNote: The long runway **softens** her resistance enough to try the basics of AI.
Still **anxious**: she expects the papers to vanish and must change field.
Values **people work**, steering her towards schools and libraries.

steps.text: Keep reporting for the weekly papers for a few more years
Retrain as a teaching assistant around year three
Ask library staff to teach her the AI basics
Save a set amount every month towards a cushion

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's two years and I'm not quick with change. What would help is someone local, at the council or the job centre, who actually sits down with you and says here are three jobs you could do. And a bit of money to tide us over while I find one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small towns when there's no local paper. People think it's just the fete and the obituaries. A local reporter is often the only person who reads the boring documents and notices when something's wrong.

headlineQuote: A local reporter is often the only person who reads the boring documents and notices when something's wrong.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old reporter** for three weekly papers covering market towns, renting with her mechanic partner.
She **never uses AI** and is slow with new things, preferring face-to-face trust over speed.
She's already **anxious** in AI Plateau and **alarmed** across most pictures, expecting to be cut.
Her fallback is **hands-on or council** work, leaning on her partner's bus depot job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone slow with change.
whatWouldHelp: A **local adviser** who sits down and names three jobs she could do.
Some **money** to tide them over while she finds one.
